segments.title: Expert contributors connect current fleets to naval history
segments.body: World Naval Review combines current naval affairs with historical context, drawing on established historians and analysts. The 2022 volume introduces contributors including Norman Friedman, David Hobbs, Richard Scott and Richard Beedall, with Conrad Waters as editor. The review then turns to the newly supplied 2026 edition, whose contents include regional fleet surveys and studies of individual ships and weapons. The selected readings cover Japan in the Asia-Pacific survey, India's INS Vikrant, and Friedman's chapter on surface-ship anti-submarine weapons.

evidence.note: The 2022 contributor list introduces the series before the 2026 edition and its selected Japan, Vikrant and ASW readings. Some additional contributor names are indistinct in the captions.

segments.summary: World Naval Review brings established naval historians and analysts together to place current fleet developments in historical context.

segments.title: World Naval Review carries on the annual-survey tradition
segments.body: World Naval Review is recommended here for the annual updating role associated with Brassey's and Jane's. Each volume gives a snapshot of naval developments at the time of publication. That makes successive editions useful for following change, while fixing each assessment to the information available that year.

evidence.note: Comparison with Brassey's and Jane's annual updating role, with the explicit qualification that each volume is a snapshot.

segments.summary: The annual volumes offer dated snapshots of naval developments, continuing a reference-book role associated with Brassey's and Jane's.

segments.title: Japan seeks more fleet lethality without more personnel
segments.body: The Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force is expanding steadily under the national security and defence strategies published in late 2022, although its growth is less dramatic than that of China's navy. Rising expenditure does not remove Japan's demographic constraint: the service must work within a headcount of roughly 45,000 personnel. The resulting force-design problem is to increase lethality within that existing workforce. The interpretation offered here connects this pressure to uncrewed systems and weapons that provide greater range or a defensive advantage. Personnel survivability is part of that reasoning.

evidence.note: The book's roughly 45,000-person constraint is followed by an interpretation connecting Japan's uncrewed systems and range advantages to personnel survivability.

segments.summary: Japan's naval expansion must increase lethality and survivability while working within a roughly fixed headcount.

segments.title: Mogami frigates sustain Japan's surface-fleet growth
segments.body: The compact, minimally crewed Mogami class combines frigate duties with uncrewed mine-countermeasures work previously assigned to dedicated vessels. Japan commissioned the seventh and eighth ships in May and June 2025, continuing a pace of roughly two deliveries per year since 2022. The year's two new surface ships produced a net increase of one major unit because an older destroyer transferred to training duties. Orders shifted in the financial year 2024 budget toward a larger upgraded variant after twelve original Mogamis had been ordered. Twelve upgraded ships were envisaged, with orders intended to finish by financial year 2028. Approving three in the 2025 budget formed part of that acceleration.

evidence.note: Net surface-fleet growth, training-role transfer, Mogami mine-countermeasures duties, two annual deliveries and the upgraded variant's 2024-2028 ordering plan.

segments.summary: The Mogami program uses rapid serial construction and small crews to expand Japan's frigate and mine-warfare capacity.

segments.title: Japan pairs a 50-combatant goal with rolling submarine production
segments.body: Rapid frigate construction supports a target of 50 surface combatants while allowing the retirement of obsolete ships with large crews. The stated target is additional to four carrier-like helicopter-carrying destroyers and two new Aegis System Equipped Vessels. The underwater force has reached 22 frontline boats, with two more assigned to training and one to trials. Its rolling replacement plan orders one submarine, delivers one and retires one after training service each year. The 2025 budget authorizes the ninth Taigei-class boat for 114 billion yen, approximately US$780 million in the figures read here. The fourth boat's March 2025 delivery and an older training submarine's withdrawal illustrate that replacement cycle. The budget's other new-ship approvals are three landing and transport vessels for the Joint Defense Force Maritime Transport Group, established on 24 March 2025.

evidence.note: The 50-combatant target excludes the four carrier-like destroyers and two Aegis vessels. Submarine totals, annual replacements, the ninth Taigei order and joint transport approvals follow.

segments.summary: Japan combines a 50-combatant target with a steady submarine replacement cycle and new joint maritime transport ships.

segments.title: Japan accelerates missiles, Aegis ships, and mine warfare
segments.body: The 2025 budget brings Tomahawk and improved Type 12 surface-to-surface missile introduction forward by a year. It also supports two Aegis System Equipped Vessels expected in 2027-2028 and funds research for eventual replacement of the four Kongo-class destroyers. Mine-warfare investment continues through the Awaji class, with a fourth arrival, two further orders and nine vessels ultimately planned. These dedicated mine-countermeasures ships supplement the frigates' mine-warfare equipment. The operational minehunter total nevertheless fell by one to 17 after a retirement and JS Ukushima's capsize and sinking following an engine-room fire.

evidence.note: Accelerated missile introduction, projected 2027-2028 Aegis arrivals, Kongo replacement research and the dedicated minehunter force's fall to 17 despite construction.

segments.summary: Japan's 2025 budget accelerates long-range missiles and Aegis work while continuing investment in dedicated minehunters.

segments.title: Regional surveys and notes create research trails
segments.body: The Asia-Pacific survey continues beyond Japan to both Koreas, Indonesia, Malaysia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. The coverage varies in length, with New Zealand receiving a short section and Singapore more detail. The notes provide specific leads to look up for further research. Readers can use the country summaries to orient themselves, then follow those notes into the supporting material.

evidence.note: The remaining country sections and detailed notes provide routes to further research.

segments.summary: Country-by-country coverage and detailed notes make the volume both a fleet summary and a starting point for further naval research.

segments.title: INS Vikrant builds Indian carrier expertise
segments.body: Judging INS Vikrant solely by its missing features overlooks the effort required to establish India's indigenous carrier-building capability. Foreign advice was bought where available, but India still had to develop and assemble the capabilities needed to design and build the ship. Carrier construction and indigenous nuclear-submarine work are presented as evidence of the country's naval industrial development. A personal procurement preference follows: a well-supported indigenous carrier program would have deserved more funding at the expense of some other projects. The reasoning concerns India's continuing capacity to develop its own ships, as well as Vikrant's immediate value.

evidence.note: Vikrant's industrial achievement, the use of foreign advice and a personal preference for greater investment in India's indigenous carrier program.

segments.summary: Vikrant matters as much for the carrier-building capability India created as for the ship's individual features.

segments.title: Vikrant exposes the cost of missing project experience
segments.body: Repeated changes to Vikrant's design and equipment contributed to schedule and cost overruns. The book attributes the underlying underestimation to insufficient institutional experience of a project at this scale. Despite attempts to establish oversight, project-management controls appear to have been inadequate and some equipment orders slipped by years. The aviation-facilities design contract was placed in April 2006, sixteen months after the design was supposed to have been completed. Finalization in January 2009 was about five years late, affecting power generation and heating, ventilation and air-conditioning requirements. The resulting procurement delay also held up phase-three construction.

evidence.note: Design revisions, first-of-kind inexperience and underestimation of project difficulty.
Qualified criticism of oversight, April 2006 contract placement, January 2009 design completion and consequences for ship systems and phase-three construction.

segments.summary: Limited experience, late design decisions and apparently weak oversight spread delays across Vikrant's systems and construction.

segments.title: A generation without building carriers erodes practical experience
segments.body: Previous shipbuilding experience does not guarantee that a country retains the ability to repeat a complex project. A twenty-year gap allows an entire generation to pass through without doing that work. An institution may remember that it built such ships while having lost much of the practical experience required to build them again. The caution applies to established builders as well as countries undertaking their first carrier.

evidence.note: A twenty-year construction gap leaves a generation without direct experience, qualifying claims that institutional memory survives automatically.

segments.summary: Long gaps between major shipbuilding projects can leave experienced institutions with a new generation that has never done the work.

segments.title: Vikrant's steel problem creates a domestic capability
segments.body: Indian naval explanations emphasize late overseas deliveries and the difficulty of persuading some domestic suppliers to join a bespoke project. The book regards part of that criticism as disingenuous in light of management weaknesses, while accepting that serious supply-chain problems existed. When planned purchases of warship-quality steel from Russia reached a commercial impasse, India's Defence Metallurgical Research Laboratory developed a domestic high-tensile formulation. The Steel Authority of India put three DMR-249 grades into production for the hull and internal structure, flight deck, and machinery-space decks. The quantity produced for the carrier is estimated at up to 30,000 tons. Establishing that capability took substantial time and added to the program's delay.

evidence.note: The book disputes parts of the supplier-blame explanation while tracing the Russian steel impasse, domestic DMR-249 production and an estimated upper quantity of 30,000 tons.

segments.summary: A failed Russian steel purchase delayed Vikrant but pushed India to develop specialized domestic warship steel.

segments.title: Vikrant's changing design drives major cost growth
segments.body: When approved in 1999, the air-defence ship proposal was expected to cost 17.3 billion rupees, approximately US$200 million at the mid-2025 exchange rates used for comparison. Its evolution into a 37,000-ton MiG-29K carrier nearly doubled the projection to 32.6 billion rupees when the revised design was approved in early 2003. Shipyard upgrades required further spending alongside the carrier itself. In July 2014, the Cabinet Committee on Security approved a much higher estimate of 193.4 billion rupees, roughly US$2.25 billion. The account treats that as an approved estimate, with no subsequent official revision identified, and judges that costs will have risen over the following decade. It therefore does not establish a final completed-program cost.

evidence.note: Cost estimates from 1999, early 2003 and July 2014, using mid-2025 exchange rates. The later increase is an assessment without a revised official total, and the shipyard-upgrade amount is unclear in the captions.

segments.summary: Growth from the original air-defence ship concept to a larger MiG-29K carrier transformed Vikrant's budget and shipyard needs.

segments.title: Vikrant's local-content figure needs context
segments.body: India estimates Vikrant's indigenous content at 76 percent, and Cochin Shipyard credits the program with demand across steel, electrical and mechanical equipment, infrastructure and services. Roughly 550 Indian vendors participated, including about 100 medium and small enterprises. That percentage needs qualification because some equipment counted as local was licensed, incorporated imported products, or was mainly assembled in India. Domestic steel production provides a more concrete example of a capability that can support future warships. The industrial base also gained experience supplying materials and equipment to modern naval standards. Designers, shipbuilders and other participants acquired practical knowledge and confidence in carrying out complex warship projects at scale.

evidence.note: The estimated 76-percent local content, 550 vendors and approximately 100 smaller enterprises, qualified by licensing and imported content. Domestic steel and accumulated construction experience are distinct gains.

segments.summary: Vikrant's claimed local content includes caveats, yet its durable gains in suppliers, steelmaking, and institutional confidence remain substantial.

segments.title: Falklands lessons lead to depth fuses for existing bombs
segments.body: Norman Friedman's surface-ship ASW chapter introduces lessons from the Falklands War. The US Navy considered a dedicated weapon comparable to Limbo, then bought depth-charge fuses for standard aircraft bombs. Adapting an existing weapon could provide the required role without introducing an entirely new weapon system. The surrounding discussion connects weapon adaptation with extending a surface ship's anti-submarine reach and mentions torpedo countermeasures.

evidence.note: The Falklands example describes consideration of a Limbo-like weapon followed by purchase of depth fuses for existing aircraft bombs, with range and torpedo countermeasures also mentioned.

segments.summary: The US Navy's purchase of depth fuses for standard aircraft bombs illustrates an alternative to introducing a dedicated ASW weapon.

segments.title: Wars of choice encouraged neglect of the submarine threat
segments.body: In this interpretation, anti-submarine warfare probably suffered most during the period when major powers expected wars of choice and no peer opponent. Aircraft and missiles remained visible threats, while submarines became easier to put out of mind. Another complacent response was to assume that submarines would get through, much as the interwar bomber was treated as unstoppable. Both attitudes evade the complications of actual warfare. The criticism concerns the assumptions behind neglecting ASW, rather than a detailed comparison of procurement budgets.

evidence.note: A qualified judgment that ASW suffered most in the wars-of-choice era, alongside an analogy with interwar assumptions about bombers.

segments.summary: ASW is judged to have suffered especially when visible air threats held attention and submarines were ignored or presumed unstoppable.

segments.title: ASROC turns sonar range into a firing solution
segments.body: The 1950s ASROC system matched the approximately 10,000-yard reliable range credited to the 5 kHz SQS-23 sonar. Its unguided ballistic rocket could carry a homing torpedo or a nuclear depth bomb. In theory, the sonar would locate a submarine accurately enough for the torpedo to acquire it after arriving at the position calculated at launch. There was no provision to adjust that aim point during the rocket's flight. ASROC was widely installed on US Navy and some foreign ships through the 1980s.

evidence.note: SQS-23 frequency and nominal direct-path range, ASROC payloads, theoretical acquisition, fixed aim point and widespread installation.

segments.summary: Early ASROC paired SQS-23 sonar range with a rocket-delivered torpedo or nuclear depth bomb, but offered no in-flight correction.

segments.title: A captain planned four ASROCs to cover submarine movement
segments.body: Alex Clarke recalls a former US Navy captain whose ship carried ASROC. Although the prescribed attack called for two weapons, the captain intended to launch four around the target. His reasoning was that submarine movement would still leave two torpedoes within acquisition range. This is a recollection of one captain's intended tactic, without evidence here that he used it in combat.

evidence.note: Alex Clarke's recollection of an unnamed captain's intended four-weapon pattern, contrasted with the prescribed two-weapon attack.

segments.summary: One captain's intended four-weapon pattern aimed to keep torpedoes within acquisition range despite a submarine moving during the attack.

segments.title: MATCH and Ikara keep the ship in the attack loop
segments.body: Britain's MATCH concept used a helicopter controlled by the attacking ship to carry the anti-submarine weapon outward. The Anglo-Australian Ikara and French Malafon used ship-controlled missiles. Radar control offered the possibility of handing the weapon to a second ship better placed to track the submarine. A later Franco-Italian follow-up based on an anti-ship cruise missile had considerably greater range, although only Italy adopted it.

evidence.note: MATCH, Ikara and Malafon exploit shipboard sonar while retaining ship control, with possible control transfer to another ship. A longer-range Franco-Italian follow-up is mentioned, but its name is indistinct.

segments.summary: Britain's MATCH helicopter and the Ikara and Malafon missiles extended an attack beyond the ship while retaining shipboard control.

segments.title: Sonar geometry caps useful ASW missile range
segments.body: Low-frequency sonar can detect beyond direct path as sound bends downward and returns at convergence-zone ranges. A convergence zone may be about five nautical miles wide, leaving too much positional uncertainty for simply firing a torpedo-carrying missile into it. Norman Friedman therefore places the generally useful ship-launched missile range near 20,000 yards, with exceptions where sound trapped in layers extends useful detection. The planned extended-range ASROC for SQS-26 was cancelled during the Vietnam War. Later VL-ASROC matched the SQS-53's roughly 20,000-yard direct-path range. Japan developed a Type 07 equivalent carrying an indigenous lightweight torpedo, while South Korea's Red Shark is described as carrying its White Shark torpedo.

evidence.note: Convergence-zone width limits targeting precision, with special propagation conditions as an exception. The ASROC development sequence and Japanese and Korean equivalents follow.

segments.summary: Long sonar detection does not automatically yield a precise firing solution, so modern ship-launched ASW missiles are matched to useful direct-path ranges.

segments.title: Long-range ASW proposals combine missile reach with local sensing
segments.body: China and India claim ASW weapons with substantially longer ranges than earlier ship-launched systems. The Chinese Yu-8's claimed 50-kilometre range suggests attacks on convergence-zone contacts or unusually long direct-path detections. An earlier US proposal would have adapted Tomahawk into a cruise missile that deployed sonobuoys in the indicated target area and monitored them while circling overhead. It would release its torpedo after those sensors supplied a suitable target. The reason for abandoning that proposal is left uncertain, with practicality and expense offered as alternatives.

evidence.note: The Yu-8's claimed 50-kilometre range and a proposed Tomahawk that would deploy and monitor sonobuoys before dropping a torpedo. The cancellation reason is explicitly uncertain.

segments.summary: The Yu-8 range claim and a proposed sonobuoy-carrying Tomahawk illustrate the sensing problem behind distant ASW attacks.

segments.title: A helicopter could retain contact while a ship supplies more weapons
segments.body: One proposed explanation for Chinese and Indian long-range ASW weapons is that they support helicopters already tracking a submarine. A helicopter that has exhausted its weapons could request a missile from a ship within range and continue holding contact. Returning to rearm would risk losing the submarine. That risk becomes especially serious when the formation is under heavy attack and has no spare helicopter to take over. This is an interpretation of the weapons' possible employment, without a claim that it describes confirmed doctrine.

evidence.note: A personal theory of ship-launched weapons supporting a helicopter that has run out of ammunition, with contact loss and unavailable relief aircraft as the operational problems.

segments.summary: A proposed use for long-range ASW missiles lets an unarmed helicopter keep tracking a submarine while its ship delivers another weapon.

segments.title: SMART's claimed range demands more precise forward sensors
segments.body: SMART is credited in the book extract with a range of 350 or 400 nautical miles, inertial navigation and midcourse updates through a data link. A suggestion that it attacks contacts from a broad underwater sensing network raises a precision problem: an approximate submarine location would be insufficient after such a long flight. The argument therefore calls for additional sensors closer to the target. Helicopters and possibly rotary UAVs with dipping sonar are proposed as candidates. Aircraft-deployed sonobuoys are another possibility, although their adequacy for the required accuracy and updating is left unresolved.

evidence.note: SMART's quoted range and guidance methods, the book's objection to broad-area sensing precision, and proposed local sensors with explicit uncertainty about sonobuoy adequacy.

segments.summary: SMART's long flight and midcourse data link make accurate sensors near the submarine central to the proposed attack system.

segments.title: Crewed helicopters may lead uncrewed ASW teams
segments.body: One forecast for future ASW hunter-killer groups puts a crewed helicopter in charge of three or four uncrewed assistants. Those aircraft would operate in a coordinated pattern with several dipping sonars. Multiple sonars are intended to make a submarine's evasion more difficult. This remains a proposed future arrangement.

evidence.note: A forecast of one crewed helicopter and three or four uncrewed assistants operating with multiple dipping sonars. The phrase following the sonar reference is unclear in the captions.

segments.summary: A future ASW hunter group could combine one crewed helicopter with several uncrewed assistants operating multiple dipping sonars.

segments.title: Mark 48 scarcity cancels a Knox-class armament plan
segments.body: Surface ASW ships once carried wire-guided torpedoes that could theoretically use the ship's long-range sonar throughout an attack. The most ambitious US proposal would have installed Mark 48 torpedo tubes on Knox-class frigates. Vietnam-era financial pressure left too few Mark 48s in production to arm both the submarine force and the frigates, so the surface-ship plan was dropped. It was not revived when US naval finances recovered.

evidence.note: Wire-guided surface torpedoes, the Knox-class Mark 48 proposal, insufficient production under Vietnam-era financial pressure, and failure to revive the idea after finances recovered.

segments.summary: A plan to arm Knox-class frigates with wire-guided Mark 48 torpedoes failed because production could not support both submarines and surface escorts.

segments.title: Shipboard ASW competes for magazine and launcher space
segments.body: A frigate has limited length and volume for weapons, and ASW is usually one of several roles competing for that space. In the 1950s and 1960s, long-range ASW weapons competed mainly with anti-aircraft armament. Anti-ship missiles and embarked helicopters later added demands on weapon stowage, hangars and flight decks. The US Mark 41 vertical launcher accommodates different roles in modular cells, including air-defence and strike missiles as well as vertical-launch ASROC and its Japanese and Korean equivalents. The limitation identified in the book is that the launcher cannot be replenished at sea, although work on that problem is acknowledged. On that basis, a ship leaves port with a set distribution of weapon functions.

evidence.note: Hull configuration, finite stowage and replenishment limit shipboard ASW weapons in a multi-role frigate.
Anti-ship missiles and helicopters intensify competition for space. Mark 41 supports mixed weapons, but the book identifies at-sea replenishment as an unresolved limitation.

segments.summary: Limited hull space and a fixed sailing load force frigates to divide weapons and aviation capacity among competing missions.

segments.title: Cruiser labels prompt an objection about destroyer-leader origins
segments.body: Norman Friedman's account places an early multi-role launcher aboard large US Navy cruisers. Alex Clarke objects to that description because the ships originated as destroyer leaders. The comment also distinguishes their mainly conventional propulsion from a nuclear-powered counterpart.

evidence.note: A disagreement over the book's large-cruiser description and the ships' destroyer-leader origins. The class name is unclear in the captions and the nuclear counterpart is not named.

segments.summary: A disagreement over cruiser terminology separates the book's designation from the ships' destroyer-leader origins.

segments.title: Changing unused VLS missiles reconfigures a ship's role
segments.body: Norman Friedman's point about replenishment at sea prompts a distinction in terminology. Alex Clarke uses reconfiguration for removing unused missiles and replacing them with a different selection. That changes the load already aboard and the missions it supports, even before the original weapons have been fired.

evidence.note: Alex Clarke distinguishes his term reconfiguration from Norman Friedman's replenishment wording by describing the exchange of unused missiles.

segments.summary: Exchanging unused missiles for different types would change a ship's mission load at sea.

segments.title: Uncrewed systems can add mass around crewed forces
segments.body: The prediction is that uncrewed systems will supply additional numbers alongside crewed platforms. This is a forecast of how future forces will gain mass, with no particular fleet size or timetable specified.

evidence.note: A closing prediction that uncrewed systems will provide mass alongside crewed systems.

segments.summary: Uncrewed systems are expected to supply additional numbers alongside crewed platforms.
